title: Didactic example — check your Python list intuition
description: A short check-your-understanding sweep on Python list semantics — the kind of standalone quiz a tutor would drop in after a 10-minute reading. Mixes single + multi-select, with a Theory section in between to set the context.

sections.title: Context — what we mean by "list" in Python

data.markdown:
## Setup

Before the quiz, recall the basics:

- A Python `list` is a **mutable, ordered, indexable** sequence.
- Slicing creates a **new list** (a shallow copy of the slice).
- Lists are passed by reference — a function that mutates its argument changes the caller's list.
- `list.append(x)` returns `None`; the mutation happens in place.

The questions below probe each of these in turn.

data.question:
What does the following snippet print?

```python
xs = [1, 2, 3]
ys = xs
ys.append(4)
print(xs)
```
options: TypeError — cannot append to xs through ys
data.explanation: `ys = xs` does not copy — both names point at the same list object, so mutating through `ys` is visible through `xs`. To copy, use `ys = xs.copy()` or `ys = xs[:]`.

data.question: Which of these are TRUE about slicing a list with `xs[a:b]`? (Pick every option that is true.)
options: Returns a NEW list — mutating the slice does not affect `xs`.
Includes index `a` and excludes index `b` (half-open interval).
Negative indices count from the end of the list.
data.explanation: Slices are half-open and produce a fresh shallow copy. Negative indices wrap from the end. Crucially, slicing **never** raises on out-of-range bounds — it just clamps and returns whatever is in range (possibly empty).

data.question:
What is the value of `xs` after this snippet?

```python
xs = [1, 2, 3]
xs = xs.append(4)
```
data.explanation: `list.append` returns `None` — it mutates in place. So `xs = xs.append(4)` first mutates the original list to `[1, 2, 3, 4]`, then immediately rebinds the name `xs` to the return value `None`, throwing away the mutated reference. This is one of the most common Python beginner footguns.

sections.title: Q4 — which of these create a true copy?

data.question: Given `xs = [1, 2, 3]`, which of these expressions create an INDEPENDENT copy that you can mutate without affecting `xs`? (Pick every option that is true.)
data.explanation: All of `xs[:]`, `xs.copy()`, `list(xs)`, and `copy.copy(xs)` create a shallow copy (new outer list, same element references). `ys = xs` is just aliasing — both names point at the same list object, so it does NOT count as a copy.
